Hanoch
HAY-nock
proper noun
Hebrew Chanok (H2585), dedicated or initiated — from chanak (H2596), to dedicate, to initiate, to train up; the same root that gives the feast of dedication its name.

Biblical Definition

Hanoch is the Authorized Version's form of a name it elsewhere renders Enoch, and it belongs in Scripture to two men distinct from Enoch the son of Jared who walked with God. The first is Hanoch the eldest son of Reuben, head of the family of the Hanochites, who went down into Egypt with Jacob and whose house was numbered in the wilderness (Gen 46:9; Num 26:5; 1Ch 5:3). The second is Hanoch a son of Midian, grandson of Abraham by Keturah, listed among the Arabian peoples descended from the patriarch (Gen 25:4; written Henoch at 1Ch 1:33). The name means dedicated, from chanak — the verb behind the dedication of a house (Deu 20:5), behind Hanukkah, the feast of the dedication of the temple, and behind the great charge to fathers: Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it (Pro 22:6). The word in that proverb is this word. To name a son Hanoch was to declare him set apart for God from the beginning, and to take on the work of training that the setting apart implies.

Origin & Era

The name of two men — the eldest son of Reuben, and a son of Midian by Keturah. It means dedicated, or trained up.

HANOCH, Hebrew Chanok, dedicated, initiated; elsewhere rendered Enoch or Henoch.

1. The eldest son of Reuben, head of the family of the Hanochites.

He went down into Egypt in the household of Jacob.

2. A son of Midian, grandson of Abraham by Keturah.

From chanak, to dedicate or train up, the verb of Proverbs 22:6.

Key Scripture

Gen 46:9 — "And the sons of Reuben; Hanoch, and Phallu, and Hezron, and Carmi."

Num 26:5 — "Reuben, the eldest son of Israel: the children of Reuben; Hanoch, of whom cometh the family of the Hanochites: of Pallu, the family of the Palluites:"

Gen 25:4 — "And the sons of Midian; Ephah, and Epher, and Hanoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All these were the children of Keturah."

1Ch 1:33 — "And the sons of Midian; Ephah, and Epher, and Henoch, and Abida, and Eldaah. All these are the sons of Keturah."

Modern Corruption

Proverbs 22:6 is read as a guarantee of outcomes; the verb means to dedicate and train, and the proverb states a rule, not a contract.

expand to see more

Train up a child in the way he should go: and when he is old, he will not depart from it has been pressed into service as an absolute promise, with the result that faithful parents of wayward children are handed a verdict of guilt they do not deserve, and presumptuous parents are handed an assurance they have no right to. A proverb is a proverb. The book of Proverbs states the ordinary course of things under God's moral government — diligence tends to profit, a soft answer tends to turn away wrath — and it is not a set of mechanical guarantees, as the book of Job and the psalms of the afflicted righteous exist in part to show.

Held rightly, the verse is a mercy. Chanak means to dedicate and to initiate: to set a child apart for God and to start him along a path, which is exactly what Christian parents are commanded to do — bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Eph 6:4). The outcome remains God's to give, for regeneration is His work and not the parent's; the training is the parent's to do, and it is not optional. The principle to recover is the division of labour: parents are responsible for the means, God is sovereign over the end, and a father who has been faithful in the first is not guilty for the second.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew Chanok (H2585), from chanak (H2596), to dedicate, to initiate, to train up.

expand to see more

Hebrew chanak (H2596) — to dedicate, initiate, train up; the verb of Proverbs 22:6 and of dedicating a new house (Deu 20:5).

Hebrew Chanok (H2585) — Hanoch or Enoch; the eldest son of Reuben (Gen 46:9) and a son of Midian (Gen 25:4).

Hebrew chanukkah (H2598) — dedication; the feast of the dedication of the temple, kept in Jerusalem (Joh 10:22).

Hebrew Qeturah (H6989) — Keturah, incense; Abraham's wife after Sarah, mother of Midian.

Greek ektrepho (G1625) — to nourish up, to bring up; bring them up in the nurture and admonition of the Lord (Eph 6:4).
